First week, a Monday: Sarika ate dinner alone in the hostel mess for the fifth day running, scrolling photos of her friends back in Guwahati. Nobody in Bengaluru knew her name.
Second week, a Saturday: a smiling senior, Sudha, sat beside her in the library. "You look like you need a proper meal. Come for our Sunday lunch." Sarika went. Twenty people clapped when she walked in. Someone had already learnt she liked fish curry. They called each other "family". She laughed more that afternoon than in the whole month before.
Fourth week, a Sunday: riding back in Sudha's car after the third lunch, Sarika realised she couldn't say what the group actually believed. Something about "the path". She didn't really care. She only knew that on Sundays, for a few hours, she stopped feeling like a stranger. When her mother called that night and asked about the lunches, Sarika answered quickly and changed the subject.

qa.a: Someone had already learnt she liked fish curry.

qa.q: Why did Sarika keep going back to the Sunday lunches?
qa.a: Sarika felt lonely in a new city, and at the lunches she felt wanted and stopped feeling like a stranger; the beliefs hardly mattered to her.

Abhinav, you've been going to those Saturday meetings since your grandfather passed. I'm not going to scold you. Let me just tell you a story.
When I was twenty, my father died in March, and by June I was a ghost at college. Then a girl from my hostel, all smiles, took my hand and brought me to a "study circle". They hugged me at the door. They brought me tea without asking. For the first time in months, when I skipped a day, someone said, "We missed you, Swati."
I didn't care what they taught. I cared that they wanted me.
It was my cousin Hema who noticed. She came to the hostel, sat on my bed and said, "I'm glad you have people. Will they still want you if you ask questions?" So at the next meeting I asked one question. The smiles went thin.
That was my turning point. The warmth had been real, but it came with a price.

qa.a: Swati's father died in March.

qa.q: Why was young Swati drawn to the study circle?
qa.a: Young Swati was grieving and lonely, and felt wanted when they hugged at the door and said 'We missed you'; the teachings hardly mattered.

qa.q: What was the turning point inside the story?
qa.a: Asking one question at the next meeting, as Hema suggested; the thin smiles showed the welcome depended on not questioning.

qa.q: How did Hema see what was happening to Swati?
qa.a: Hema was glad Swati had people but worried about the price, so Hema asked a gentle question instead of scolding.

The hostel emptied for the Diwali break, and Nazia's train ticket home to Lucknow was still waitlisted. On the second silent evening, rain hammering the tin roof of the canteen, she was the only one eating.
Lalit, a cheerful volunteer who had been handing out leaflets near the library all month, shook out his umbrella and sat opposite. "Nobody should be alone during the holidays. We're doing a free weekend retreat. Food, music, good people. Bus leaves at seven."
She hesitated. She didn't even know what the retreat was about.
"Doesn't matter," Lalit said, smiling. "You'll feel at home."
At the retreat that night, thirty strangers learnt her name within an hour. Someone wrapped a shawl around her shoulders. For the first time since she'd come to Delhi, she fell asleep without that heavy lump in her chest.
The next morning her phone showed two missed calls from Ammi. She had forgotten to tell anyone where she was.

Jyoti, you once asked me why I never talk about my college years. Here's why.
At nineteen I joined a "leadership fellowship" in Hyderabad. At first it was one Saturday a month. Then every Saturday. Then Friday nights too, because the "inner circle" studied special texts nobody outside could understand. Then a small monthly "contribution". Then a bigger one. Each step felt like nothing.
By twenty-one I had stopped visiting home. My elder brother, Irfan, kept asking questions, and the fellowship told me doubters were testing my strength. So I stopped answering his calls.
One day Irfan simply turned up at my hostel with a tiffin of Ammi's biryani. He didn't argue. He said, "Farhan, eat first. Then tell me what a normal week looks like for you now." I started listing it. Halfway through, I heard myself. Every hour, every rupee, every friend, gone one small piece at a time.

qa.a: A tiffin of Ammi's biryani.

qa.q: How did young Farhan feel while listing a normal week aloud?
qa.a: Young Farhan was startled and shaken, hearing for the first time how every hour, rupee and friend had gone piece by piece.

qa.q: What choice inside the story became the turning point?
qa.a: Irfan turning up with food and asking for a description of a normal week instead of arguing; saying it aloud let Farhan see the whole change.

qa.a: Irfan was likely worried and hurt, yet chose patience, coming with food rather than anger.
